main.title: Codebreaker
main.summary: Codebreaker is a puzzle video game released in 1978 by Atari, Inc. for the Atari VCS (later renamed the Atari 2600).

cards.text: Codebreaker is a puzzle video game released in 1978 by Atari, Inc. for the Atari VCS (later renamed the Atari 2600). It was in the first wave of Atari VCS games to follow the original nine launch titles. It was one of three cartridges to accompany the introduction of the Atari keyboard controller, an add-on launched in response to claims of false advertising that the VCS is a "computer" (the other two were Hunt & Score and Brain Games).
The cartridge contains Bagels, Nim and Mastermind, each with six variations. Players use the keyboard controller to enter the numerical choices required by the selected game.
The games may be played in single-player mode, or in a two-player mode where the players play together.

Contemporary reviewers were relatively positive about the game but all mentioned its similarity to Mordecai Meirowitz's Mastermind. The British computer games magazine TV Gamer, described it as "not the most original game" but also described it as an enjoyable brain-teaser. Personal Computing Magazine described it as "[b]ased on the Mastermind concept".

main.title: Avalanche
main.summary: Avalanche is a 1978 arcade game designed by Dennis Koble and released by Atari. Players catch falling rocks with paddles that become fewer and smaller as the challenge accelerates.

cards.text: Avalanche is a 1978 arcade game designed by Dennis Koble and released by Atari. The player catches falling rocks with a controllable set of paddles. As the rocks fall faster, the paddles diminish in number and size, leaving less room to intercept them.

A port of the game was developed by Koble to help kickstart the Atari Program Exchange. The game influenced the Activision game Kaboom! (1981) for the Atari 2600, which went on to be one of the top-selling Atari 2600 video games. In 2025, Atari released official ports for the 2600 and 7800 consoles.

One or two players can take alternating turns. Six rows of rocks begin above a six-level catching platform. Clearing a row removes one level of the platform, and later rocks become smaller and faster. Each rock caught before it reaches the ground earns points. Reaching the required score allows the player to continue after losing the initial game.

Dennis Koble joined Atari in 1976 as its fourth programmer. During roughly two and a half years working on arcades, his projects included Sprint 2 and Dominos. Avalanche was his last published arcade game before he moved to the company's consumer division.

Avalanche started out as a game about eggs and baskets called Catch. The game initially performed poorly with test audiences which led the game to be changed to be about collecting rocks and was eventually renamed Avalanche. Ed Logg, who started at Atari in February 1978, was assigned to projects that were either completed or started by Koble, who was moving on to the consumer division of the company. Logg said that by the time he got to Avalanche, it was about to go into production and his job was to focus on working on Koble's incomplete and unreleased arcade game Dirt Bike.

Avalanche is housed in a custom cabinet that includes two large lit start buttons and a rotary controller. The side art and bezel feature groupings of rocks with extending lines meant to convey the motion of falling rocks. The screen is black and white with two colored strips to provide colored rows of graphics as in Breakout.

The circuit board is based on the 6502 CPU, with game code stored in multiple ROMs. All game text is selectable to 4 different languages: English, French, German, or Spanish. Avalanche also has a built-in self-test diagnostic program that displays all microprocessor and memory functions, including the operator switches and functions.

Avalanche was shipped to the public in April 1978. Paul Drury of Retro Gamer described Avalanche as a moderate success at the arcades. In the early 1980s, Atari, Inc. supported their 8-bit computers with the Atari Program Exchange (APX). The APX solicited software written by Atari users and sold the best via  mail order catalogs.  Koble said to get the ball rolling on the project, he submitted a video game port of Avalanche, followed by two adventure games: Chinese Puzzle and Sultan's Palace.

main.title: Mystery Mansion
main.summary: Mystery Mansion is a text adventure written in 1978–1981 by Bill Wolpert while at the Naval Undersea Warfare Center in Keyport, Washington.

cards.text: Mystery Mansion is a text adventure written in 1978–1981 by Bill Wolpert while at the Naval Undersea Warfare Center in Keyport, Washington. It originally ran only on the HP HP-1000 minicomputer on the RTE (Real Time Executive) operating system, but was later ported by persons unknown to run under MPE (Multiprocessing Executive) on the HP-3000. Although the development dates make it contemporaneous with other seminal interactive fiction games such as Adventure and Dungeon (which went on to become the Zork series from Infocom), it remains relatively unknown due to the specialized computers and operating systems on which it ran.

The object of the single-player game is to find one's way through a run-down, foreboding mansion in order to find various treasures, solve a murder, and avoid getting "killed" in the process all before the mansion is destroyed by fire at midnight to end the game. In addition to the 3 rooms x 3 rooms x 3 stories cube-shaped mansion, there are gardens, tunnels, nefarious characters, and other obstacles to make one's way through or around.

Two C-language ports exist, one by James Garnett while a graduate student at the University of Colorado, and another by Bob Sorem of the University of Minnesota. The former is a line-by-line exact port in K&R-style C that runs on most Unix-flavor operating systems, while the latter is an adaptation with features not in Wolpert's original in Borland C that runs only under MS-DOS/Windows.

main.title: Home Run
main.summary: Home Run is a 1978 baseball video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for the Atari 2600 (originally known as the Atari Video Computer System).

cards.text: Home Run is a 1978 baseball video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for the Atari 2600 (originally known as the Atari Video Computer System). It was the first baseball-themed game released for an Atari platform. The game received mostly negative critical reception due to its unrealistic portrayal of the sport. It was one of the games used by console competitor Mattel to show the quality improvement of Intellivision sports games over the Atari VCS.

Teams have only one to three players, and the fielders must run with the ball to tag players out, with throwing of the ball to force players out not being possible. There is no pitcher's mound, with the pitcher instead standing at second base. The game lacks fly balls and independent fielders.

Depending on the selected game mode, only zero to two infielders are present in the game, and when either the pitcher or one of the infielders catches the ball everyone but the baserunners and the ball-catcher instantly disappears from view. The home team has to bat at the bottom of the 9th inning regardless of whether they are winning or not, and there is no extra innings if the game is tied.
Home Run was designed and programmed by Bob Whitehead, who went on to found Activision, and David Rolfe. The cover art was designed by Cliff Spohn.

According to a 1978 New York Times interview with Nolan Bushnell, the engineer who was first assigned to develop the game didn't know the rules of the sport of baseball. As a result, in an initial version of the game if the player failed to hit the ball they were awarded a ball rather than a strike.
A television advertising campaign for the game (and the Atari VCS as a whole) was fronted by Pete Rose.
The game was one of the games used in advertisements by console competitor Mattel to show the quality improvement of Intellivision sports games over the Atari VCS.

A review in the December 1982 issue of JoyStik magazine was heavily critical of the game, stating that it was "nothing like real baseball", and describing the graphics as "primitive". The 1984 Software Encyclopedia published by Electronic Games magazine was similarly critical of the game, saying that it lacks "the "feel" of real sports action", and giving it an overall rating of 4/10. Writing in The Player's Strategy Guide to Atari VCS Home Video Games, Electronic Games editors Arnie Katz and Bill Kunkel called the game, "so pared down from the original sport that it only barely qualifies as a baseball simulation," stating that, "it might more accurately be called 'Video Stickball'."

A December 2000 review by Patrick Wong in Classic Gamer magazine panned the game, describing it as (together with Atari's Golf) "two of the worst games ever made". Wong criticised the "boring" graphics, the small number of fielders deployable in the game, and the unrealistic gameplay, and summed the game up by saying "Gamers looking for a real baseball experience will have to look elsewhere". A review in the January/February 2003 issue of Digital Press was overwhelmingly negative, describing it as "a big stinker", "one of the worst games ever designed" with graphics that are "inexcusably bad". Bret Weiss writing in Classic Home Video Games, 1972–1984: A Complete Reference Guide praised the variety of the options for pitching but found the graphics and gameplay lack-lustre. Kieren Hawken writing in The A–Z of Atari 2600 Games: Volume 2 criticised the excessively basic game-play and graphics and compared it negatively to later baseball games developed for the Atari 2600 where the developers had better utilised the platform's resources.

main.title: Dungeon Campaign
main.summary: Dungeon Campaign is a video game written by Robert Clardy and released in 1978, later published commercially by Clardy's company Synergistic Software in 1979.

cards.text: Dungeon Campaign is a video game written by Robert Clardy and released in 1978, later published commercially by Clardy's company Synergistic Software in 1979. It was created for the Apple II platform and is derived from Gary J. Shannon's Dragon Maze. Dungeon Campaign is considered one of the first microcomputer-based adventure video games.

Clardy incorporated themes from Dungeons & Dragons into the game, which later was included as a side quest within Odyssey: The Compleat Apventure, a multi-part adventure / role-playing video game also written by Clardy and released in 1980.

In the game, the player uses the keyboard to navigate a party of thirteen adventurers, including one elf and one dwarf, through the dreaded Totmacher Castle dungeon consisting of four randomly generated maze levels, which are connected by pits and stairways. The player collects treasures as they progress through the dungeon and may encounter traps and other menaces, including monsters and sorcerers. The sole exit is on the lowest level. The elf and dwarf are included to warn the player of nearby traps and to map the dungeon as it is explored, respectively; the other anonymous adventurers provide a hit point system to keep track of damage incurred from the various traps and other hostile characters.
Although reaching the exit is relatively easy, the game uses the treasures collected during the adventure to provide a final score.

Shortly after purchasing his first computer, Robert Clardy began modifying the code for Dungeon Maze, an Integer BASIC program published in the Apple II Reference Manual (1978) which included a routine to randomly generate a maze. Clardy added multiple levels and a party system.

Initially, Clardy gave away copies of the game to members of his local user group, the Apple Puget Sound Program Library Exchange; their enthusiastic reception encouraged him to add more features and, after completing a follow-up game using the Apple II's high-resolution mode, Wilderness Campaign, in December 1978, packaged both games together for a commercial release under Synergistic Software, the company he founded with his wife, Ann Dickens Clardy.
Gregg Williams reviewed Dungeon Campaign in 1980 for Byte, calling it one of his favorite games for Apple II.

main.title: Frogs
main.summary: Frogs is a 1978 action video game developed and published by Gremlin Industries for arcades.

cards.text: Frogs is a 1978 action video game developed and published by Gremlin Industries for arcades. It featured a jumping character (predating Donkey Kong by three years) with graphics "projected" by laying the monitor flat on its back and reflecting the computer-generated graphics of the frogs and flies toward the player via a mirror at a 45-degree angle. The game's graphics were actually generated and shown backward, so the mirror reflection would show letters and numbers properly. The game was distributed by Sega in Japan.

The player controls a frog on lilypads and attempts to catch (with the frog's tongue and while jumping) various insects (butterflies and dragonflies) worth different numbers of points in a set amount of time.

In 1980, Adventure International published a similar game with varying names–Frog, Frogs, Frog on a Log–for the TRS-80. In this version the player controls a large frog that moves left or right along a log.
Mattel released Frogs and Flies for the Atari 2600, which was renamed Frog Bog for the Intellivision version. Both were published in 1982.

main.title: Tarn Adams
main.subtitle: Tarn Adams and the Game That Simulates Before It Explains
main.summary: Tarn Adams was born on April 17, 1978 and grew up programming alongside his brother Zach.

cards.heading: Tarn Adams and the Game That Simulates Before It Explains
cards.text: Tarn Adams was born on 17 April 1978 and grew up programming with his brother Zach. Their best-known project is Dwarf Fortress, begun in the early 2000s and developed over decades. It generates geography, history, creatures and relationships before the player starts building a fortress. Tarn's background in mathematics accompanies an interest in detailed rules whose interactions can produce events the designers did not script individually.

cards.heading: Programming Before Calling It a Profession
cards.text: Tarn and Zach learned to program while young and made games together. Tarn continued his projects while studying mathematics through a doctorate. He later left academia to work on games, bringing an interest in precisely defined relationships and interacting systems. Dwarf Fortress gave that interest a setting with many creatures and processes operating at once.

cards.heading: Dwarf Fortress Starts as a Side Project and Becomes a World
cards.text: Dwarf Fortress began as a smaller project alongside other ideas the brothers were pursuing. Managing several miners and retaining detail in a persistent world grew into systems for civilisations, geology, history and creatures with individual traits. Each addition had to work with the existing rules. Those interactions opened further possibilities, contributing to a project that continued expanding over decades.

cards.heading: Hit Points Are Not Enough
cards.text: Adams has questioned using hit points when a single number removes consequences that could make a story interesting. Dwarf Fortress models body parts, materials, wounds and temperature. An injured creature may lose the use of a limb or respond to a particular physical condition. That detail makes the system harder to develop and explain, while allowing an encounter to produce more specific and unexpected outcomes.

main.title: Space Invaders
main.subtitle: Pressure becomes a rhythm
main.summary: Tomohiro Nishikado's descending formation made an entire screen feel like a threat.

cards.heading: A formation under pressure
cards.text: Space Invaders is an arcade game designed by Tomohiro Nishikado for Taito, first presented at a trade exhibition on 16 June 1978. Its alien formation, protective shelters and accelerating pace create increasing pressure as the player clears the screen. The popularity that followed carried the game beyond dedicated arcades into places such as Japanese coffee shops.

cards.heading: Characters made from pixels
cards.text: Nishikado's game shows how recognisable characters can emerge from tiny groups of pixels. The aliens are a repeating system and individual visual identities at the same time.

features.title: Pressure across the screen
features.summary: Nishikado shaped a challenge people could study.

cards.heading: Clearing the last target
cards.text: Tomohiro Nishikado liked the demand that Breakout placed on its player: every block had to disappear before the next stage. The difficult last target and increasing speed interested him as much as the bat and ball. In his 2000 interview, he described wanting to retain those qualities while changing the pictures. Space Invaders made the remaining targets active opponents. Clearing the screen could become more urgent as it became less crowded, giving the final few enemies a different weight from the initial formation.

cards.heading: A risky discovery
cards.text: Nishikado recalled watching a skilled player survive directly beneath the lowest enemies. Their shots began slightly in front of their bodies, leaving a gap that made the Nagoya attack possible. The technique took advantage of a programming oversight. Watching it gave Nishikado information about a behaviour he had not intended when building the game.

cards.heading: Drawing an alien's movement
cards.text: A separate 2008 interview describes a small tool behind the familiar figures. Nishikado created a way to test two-pattern sprite animation and adjusted the designs on screen with a light pen. The repeating invaders were therefore worked out as moving pictures, not only as rows of targets. His account also recalls translating American technical documentation and building development equipment when a professional workstation was too expensive. Before he could decide how an alien should move, he needed a practical way to experiment with it.

cards.heading: Finding a good machine
cards.text: Yoichi Wada remembered the game from the other side of its cabinet. As a student, he sought cafes with genuine Taito tables and controls that had not worn down through constant play. Nishikado explained that the table format had existed before Space Invaders, although its popularity helped carry those cabinets into more cafes. The formation on the screen was only part of this encounter. The condition of a joystick and the space around a table could determine where people chose to spend another evening playing.

main.title: Koei
main.subtitle: Koei Turns History into a System to Manage
main.summary: On July 25, 1978 Yōichi and Keiko Erikawa founded Koei.

cards.heading: Koei Turns History into a System to Manage
cards.text: Yōichi and Keiko Erikawa founded Koei on 25 July 1978. The company initially worked with computers and business software before developing a catalogue known for historical strategy. Nobunaga's Ambition and Romance of the Three Kingdoms asked players to manage territories, resources and officers while pursuing military power. These series became long-running parts of Koei's identity as its range of games expanded.

cards.heading: From business computers to entertainment software
cards.text: Koei's move into entertainment drew on its experience with computers and software. Historical campaigns could make use of a machine's ability to store information, calculate outcomes and present choices. Players could decide how to balance harvests, budgets and military needs while the computer handled the figures behind them. This made home computers a useful setting for the company's increasingly detailed strategy games.

cards.heading: Nobunaga's Ambition makes the Sengoku period governable
cards.text: Beginning in 1983, Nobunaga's Ambition placed players in Japan's Sengoku period. Running a territory was part of the military campaign: an army needed resources, and an attack could draw attention away from other responsibilities. Later entries expanded the systems while retaining the link between land, government and conquest. Historical names, geography and rivalries provided a starting situation whose outcome could change through the player's decisions.

cards.heading: Romance of the Three Kingdoms broadens the scale of historical storytelling
cards.text: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, launched in 1985, brings Koei's strategy design to the China of the celebrated historical novel. Territory matters, but government also depends on people: recruiting officers, assigning responsibilities and retaining their loyalty become part of building power. Characters' abilities make relationships a resource distinct from money or soldiers. Across changing perspectives and systems, the series retains this connection between administration and individual lives. The past becomes something players can renegotiate. Its protagonists remain recognizable, while alliances and decisions can lead a campaign away from the sequence of events a reader already knows.

main.title: Neil Druckmann
main.subtitle: Neil Druckmann: Build a Point of View, Then Question It
main.summary: Neil Druckmann, born on 5 December 1978, is a writer, designer and director associated with Naughty Dog and The Last of Us.

cards.heading: Neil Druckmann: Build a Point of View, Then Question It
cards.text: Neil Druckmann was born on 5 December 1978. His career spans programming, design, writing and creative direction at Naughty Dog, with projects including Jak, Uncharted, The Last of Us and its sequel. He studied entertainment technology at Carnegie Mellon before developing games that connect character relationships with exploration and action. He later worked on the television adaptation of The Last of Us with Craig Mazin.

cards.heading: Before Directing, Learn to Be Changed by Others
cards.text: At Carnegie Mellon's Entertainment Technology Center, Druckmann worked on rapid projects with people from different disciplines. He described learning to accept criticism and change his approach through that collaboration. One rejected university presentation contained elements that later developed into The Last of Us. The experience helped shape his view that a director's ideas should be open to changes contributed by other members of a team.

cards.heading: A New Team Forms Around a Risky Proposal
cards.text: Druckmann and Bruce Straley described having to win support inside Naughty Dog and PlayStation for The Last of Us. The darker new property needed to make Joel and Ellie's relationship work through exploration, combat, limited resources and quieter travel. The team developed companion responses, animation and transitions that kept the other character present during play. Their relationship depended on repeated behaviour as well as the story's staged scenes.

cards.heading: The Story Also Passes Through What the Controller Allows
cards.text: Discussing The Last of Us Part II, Druckmann distinguished literal realism from making an action feel convincing. A controller provides a limited set of inputs, so the team selects which movements and responses the player can perform. Ellie's animation, mobility, violence and interactions with enemies all contribute to how she is experienced during play. Writing, performance and level design work alongside those systems.

cards.heading: A Strong Vision Should Not Remain One Person's Property
cards.text: Druckmann recalled once imagining direction as moving people and resources towards a complete image in his head. His later approach gave collaborators more room to reinterpret and improve that idea. Large productions require decisions across animation, programming, sound, levels and other departments. Sharing a recognisable direction gives those teams a basis for judging their own solutions while contributing ideas the director had not anticipated.

cards.heading: Changing Medium Means Accepting That Some Solutions Do Not Travel
cards.text: Druckmann worked with Craig Mazin on the television adaptation of The Last of Us as co-creator, producer and episode director. The game's relationships develop across exploration, optional dialogue and repeated actions. Television builds them through performance, editing and the duration of episodes. Druckmann described working with Mazin as an opportunity for another writer to change familiar material while continuing to develop its characters and themes.
